‘Resident Evil’ is a faithful homage to the original video game

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:16
Instaread
‘Resident Evil’ trades the action of the 2000s adaptations for a funny but truly scary horror
Photo courtesy of Resident Evil’s official Instagram
By Francisco Aguirre-Ghiso, Assistant Arts Editor
September 29, 2026

Zach Cregger, director of “Barbarian” (2022) and “Weapons” (2025), continues his successful horror streak with a refreshing adaptation of the video game “Resident Evil.” The movie feels much more connected to the franchise’s survival horror roots than the earlier action adaptations of the 2000s and 2010s.

The “Resident Evil” franchise is a Japanese action/horror video game series centered around the wrongdoings of the Umbrella Corporation, a defense contractor. The Umbrella Corporation develops and often accidentally releases bioweapons into Raccoon City, an isolated mountain city, where they have a secret underground lab.

The franchise has taken many turns, with the original installments being fixed-camera survival horror games. The games in the late 2000s and early 2010s were more action-based, before reverting back to survival horror in the late 2010s.

In the “Resident Evil” film, Cregger and screenwriter Shay Hatten pay homage to the survival horror roots of the franchise. The film, while genuinely frightening, successfully integrates humor through the performance of Austin Abrams, who proves something of a reluctant protagonist.

The film follows Bryan, a hospital courier played by Abrams. Bryan finds himself stuck in a zombie apocalypse when he takes a job to deliver an unknown package to the hospital in a distant mountain city. He soon finds himself implicated in a plot to save the city while trying to survive the numerous monsters in the city and surrounding areas.

Abrams’ charming everyman performance makes the movie excel. He portrays Bryan as terrified, awkward around weaponry and seemingly useless. Bryan’s relatability and how he manages to survive the plot of the movie without seeming overly skilled or unrealistically lucky is what makes Abrams’ performance something to praise.

The first half of this film is a barren, snowy wasteland that Bryan must traverse to get to Raccoon City. This quiet setting is the perfect environment to build suspense and craft excellent jump scares. An empty household, a snowy forest at night and a frozen field illuminated only by police car lights are some of the places where Bryan initially runs into danger. All of these empty, quiet spaces are suddenly violated by some creature jumping at the screen faster than we can process, and it really gets under the viewers’ skin.

Later, as Bryan gets to Raccoon City, the scares become a little less suspenseful and closer to body horror, which helps the movie transition to more action-based second and third acts. Things no longer hide from sight but chase Bryan openly; their forms are more like creatures from “The Thing” than a typical zombie.

However, the movie loses a little bit of steam here, and Cregger proves once again that he has trouble with third acts and endings. By the time Bryan gets to the hospital in Raccoon City, the chase has become tedious. Bryan’s lack of skill, however relatable, becomes somewhat annoying. If the film was to stick to the suspense and grounded horror of the first act, or spread the suspense out a little more through the acts, this movie might have avoided the frustrating ending that we were left with.

Nonetheless, “Resident Evil” stands out for its similarity to the video game design and its inclusion of video game tropes.  The film’s cinematography, for example, uses first-person camera angles to mirror the visuals of the video game.

Cregger also designed the plot to move like a video game, with different levels, areas and obstacles that need to be overcome before Bryan can move on. He upgrades his weapons throughout the movie, starting with a pistol and finishing with a submachine gun, reflecting the classic “level-up” systems of survival horror video games. All these things nod to video game culture and tropes that have entered the cultural zeitgeist.

It is this dedication to homage that makes this movie such a noteworthy entry into the modern horror movie canon. Video games tend to be shunned as pastimes for nerds and children rather than a genuine storytelling vehicle. By drawing directly from the video game’s design and plot devices, Cregger demonstrates how video games can be a valuable form of storytelling.

The popularity of horror has only risen in past years, with movies like “Obsession” (2025) and “Backrooms” (2026) bringing swaths of people to cinemas, and TV shows like “The Last of Us” (2023-) proving that horror video games are a great genre to extract adaptations. “Resident Evil” only furthers the argument that video games, especially horror video games, are places to pull real artistic inspiration from.

“Resident Evil” is also a great film on its own, even for viewers with little to no experience with video games. It is not tied up with nerdy jargon or niche references, and you don’t need to know anything about the “Resident Evil” series to enjoy it. It’s a scary, gory and entertaining horror that also happens to be inspired by horror video games.

Despite its lackluster ending, the “Resident Evil” film has proven to be an exceptionally strong adaption of a video game to film. Perhaps the trend of video game adaptations will lead to studios looking at the medium for further inspiration and treating video games as a respectable form of storytelling.

Francisco Aguirre-Ghiso can be reached at faguirreghis@umass.edu.
